SoilSense

Soil-erosion risk, a ranked work list with reasons, and season-by-season monitoring for the whole of Assam. Built on the same data backbone that already runs two live hazard forecasts in Arunachal Pradesh.

Priority list and field kit

Monitoring: bare ground every dry season, 2019–2026

In the hills, jhum plots are cleared in winter and burned in March–April; the ground stays bare until the crop grows after the monsoon starts. The monsoon's heavy rain falls on whatever the dry season left bare, so that is the season SoilSense measures: every 100 m square, from Sentinel-2's 10 m pictures, 1 February – 30 April, every year.

Land seen clearly each season: 2019 100%, 2020 100%, 2021 100%, 2022 100%, 2023 100%, 2024 100%, 2025 100%, 2026 100%. Squares too cloudy are left blank, never guessed.

Each year's bare ground also re-runs the recipe ("loss with this year's cover"), and the catchments that got barer are listed. Flags for new bare ground on a steep slope are held back until they pass the tests on the Checks page; the measured bare ground is shown meanwhile.

Two errors caught before any result existed

1 · The usual rain formula reads 91% low in Assam

Most Indian erosion studies turn annual rainfall into rain strength with one formula. At Guwahati, the only place with a published measured value, it gives a tenth of the real figure. We use the satellite-based InRESatE map (−5%), keep IRED alongside, and tested both against 40 rain gauges.

2 · The national 250 m map barely responds to slope

Our slope factor rises 500-fold from flat land to steep hills; the national map's rises about twofold. That is why the national map rates western Assam's plains among India's most erodible, while ours puts the hills (Dima Hasao, the Karbi hills, the hills of south Kamrup and Cachar) first.

How it is built

  • The data backbone is the core. Each source is fetched by a script and stored untouched, with its source, licence, link, date and checksum. Every layer is fitted to one 100 m grid. A region switch moved it from Arunachal Pradesh to Assam in about four weeks; the live Arunachal forecasts are re-checked after every change to shared code.
  • The recipe is transparent. RUSLE, the standard used in Indian soil conservation, with each factor kept as its own layer, so an officer can see why a place ranks high.
  • Machine learning where it earns its place: classifying land cover from Sentinel-2, and a correction layer trained on field findings once enough exist, tested on areas held out from training.
  • Outputs open anywhere: GeoTIFF, GeoPackage, KML, GeoJSON, CSV, in WGS84 or UTM 46N; a web app that needs no installation.

Proof that the backbone works: two live products in Arunachal Pradesh

SoilSense is the third product on the same backbone and the first in a second state. The same team, the same pipeline, the same way of testing.

Pilot, to agree with the department

Dima Hasao and the Karbi hills (steep, jhum, erosion a known concern), plus one foothill belt for contrast. A field protocol dated before any visit: blind points stratified across classes and top-ranked catchments; teams record rills, gullies, bare soil, sediment and existing works without seeing the map's class; agreement measured against a pass mark set in advance.

Data

Built on open data: Copernicus DEM GLO-30, SoilGrids (CC-BY), ESA WorldCover (CC-BY), Sentinel-2 via Google Earth Engine, InRESatE and IRED rain-strength maps (CC-BY), HydroSHEDS, Survey of India outline. Used for comparison only, never redistributed: the IIT Delhi national erosion map (IWED), India's soil-erodibility map (ISED), NRSC's land-degradation map (Bhuvan). Ours: the backbone code, region switch, ranking and reasons, change detection, checks, app and the checked local record.
